name: Master Cleanse / juice cleanse
lead: The Master Cleanse, also called the lemonade diet, is a modified juice fast in which followers consume no solid food and instead drink a mixture of lemon juice, maple syrup and cayenne pepper in water, along with tea and a daily salt-water drink. It was marketed by Stanley Burroughs from the 1940s and revived by his 1976 book The Master Cleanser.[1] Juice cleanses more broadly restrict a person to fruit and vegetable juices for a period of usually one to seven days.[2]

Proponents describe such cleanses as a way to remove toxins, reset the body and lose weight quickly, and in appearance communities they are sometimes used to reduce bloating or look leaner before a event or a diet phase.[1][2] Dietitians and health organisations report that the detoxification claims are unsupported by scientific evidence and that any weight lost is typically regained.[1][2]

paras: In the Master Cleanse, adherents eat no food, drinking a lemonade made with maple syrup and cayenne pepper plus herbal tea, and begin each morning with a salt-water flush intended to prompt bowel movements.[1] Juice fasting is a broader category in which only fruit and vegetable juices are consumed.[2]

Burroughs first promoted the diet in the 1940s and republished it in 1976.[1] Earlier, in 1936, Norman W. Walker designed the first mechanical juicer and promoted a raw, mostly liquid diet, and in the 1990s Jay Kordich popularised juicing through television infomercials.[2] Interest in the Master Cleanse surged in 2006 when singer Beyonce discussed it on The Oprah Winfrey Show.[1]

Nutritionists quoted in encyclopedic summaries class the Master Cleanse as a fad diet and note that it is low in protein, fats, vitamins and minerals and relies on carbohydrate for calories.[1] The daily laxative component can cause electrolyte imbalance and disrupt the gut microbiome, and prolonged use could lead to severe metabolic acidosis, which can cause coma or death.[1]

For juice fasts, a dietitian has described the concept of detox as a marketing idea rather than a physiological process, the American Cancer Society says there is no scientific evidence that juice-only fasting provides health benefits, and Harvard Health notes no published research supports their safety or effectiveness.[2] Listed risks include metabolic crises in people with undiagnosed diabetes, dizziness from blood pressure drops, diarrhea with dehydration, protein or calcium deficiency in long fasts, muscle loss and fat regain afterwards.[2] Fasting in general can cause dangerous drops in sodium, potassium and magnesium, and refeeding can cause its own electrolyte problems.[3]

T Nation threads mention juice cleanses mostly in passing: one contest-prep log includes a half-joking plan to detox with a juice cleanse before stepping on stage, and another poster lists a juice cleanse among fad approaches people choose over steady training and eating.[4][5] Another member jokes about the Master Cleanse in a forum aside.[6]
No studies found. The sources reviewed cite no clinical trials of the Master Cleanse itself; commentary relies on expert opinion and general knowledge of fasting and nutrition.[1][2]

timeline.event: Norman W. Walker designs the first mechanical juicer and promotes a liquid raw diet.[2]
Stanley Burroughs begins marketing the lemonade fast.[1]
Beyonce discusses the diet on The Oprah Winfrey Show, boosting interest.[1]

lore.intro: Cleanses and juice fasts come up in lifting and physique communities as quick de-bloating or leanness tactics. On T Nation, a poster joking about contest prep says he will 'go on a juice cleanse detox' to get ready for the stage, and others cite juice cleanses as an example of looking for an easy route to weight loss.[4][5]

claims.claim: A cleanse removes toxins and resets the body.
claims.believers: Promoters say periodic juice or lemonade fasts cleanse the body and allow it to heal itself.[1][2]
claims.experts: Dietitians describe detox as a marketing idea, and no published evidence shows toxin removal.[1][2]

claims.claim: A cleanse produces fast weight loss and a leaner look.
claims.believers: Followers report rapid scale-weight drops over several days.[1]
claims.experts: Commentators say weight loss is typically temporary and regained after stopping, and that muscle loss can occur.[1][2]

claims.believers: Proponents present them as gentle and natural.[2]
claims.experts: One encyclopedic summary calls short-term harm unlikely but lists electrolyte, glucose and deficiency risks, particularly with laxative use or in people with diabetes.[1][2]

card.summary: Lemon-syrup or juice-only fasts used for quick de-bloating; medical sources report no evidence for detox claims and temporary weight loss.
card.aka: Lemonade diet, lemon detox, juice fast
card.note: Electrolyte imbalance and nutrient deficiency are listed risks of prolonged use.

quick.overview:
A cleanse means living on a restrictive liquid diet for days, either the Master Cleanse (lemon, maple syrup, cayenne) or fruit and vegetable juices.

Promoters say it detoxifies and slims; dietitians and health bodies report no evidence of detoxification and note that lost weight is usually regained.
quick.mechanism: Calorie and nutrient intake is cut sharply; some versions add a salt-water laxative drink. Quick scale drops generally reflect fluid, gut contents and stored glycogen rather than fat, according to general nutrition sources.
quick.risks: Listed risks include electrolyte disturbance, low blood sugar events in people with diabetes, dizziness, diarrhea, protein or calcium deficiency, muscle loss and rebound weight. Prolonged use of the Master Cleanse has been linked in theory to metabolic acidosis.

chain: Solid food is replaced by lemonade or juices for a few days
Gut contents, fluid and glycogen drop
Scale weight falls and the midsection looks flatter
angle.text: People use cleanses as a short reset before an event, photo or diet phase, aiming for a flatter stomach and leaner look. Quick scale drops are generally described as reflecting fluid and gut contents rather than fat.
